response:
Diagnosis after generation 5 — the archive has produced its first signal with *all three* forms of evidence aligned: Inventory Buildup Against A Maturity Wall (fmb -2.87, alpha -3.2%, t=-3.09, raw Sharpe -0.32). That result settles the question that has dominated this search. The maturity-wall conditioner (dlc/lt) generates the largest and most reliable alphas in the archive (-5.4%/t=-5.23 with peak-distance capacity, -4.9%/t=-4.07 with intangible intensity), but on its own those pairings carry zero cross-sectional slope and no raw return spread, because their investment legs are *contraction states* that fight the asset-growth effect in the body of the distribution. When the same conditioner is paired with a **flow of resources into illiquid assets**, the slope, the alpha and the raw spread all line up. The economics are clean: rollover risk becomes lethal precisely when the firm has just locked its liquidity into assets it cannot convert. This generation consolidates on that mechanism along three dimensions — broader lock-up measurement (S1), state versus flow (S2), and a sharper composite conditioner (S3) — plus the one positive-side construction that worked (S4), the broadest asset-side liquidity-mismatch reading (S6), and one genuinely new operating axis (S5).

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Working Capital Lock-Up At The Maturity Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(GROWTH(invt, 1), GROWTH(SUB(act, che), 1))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: Liquidity locked into goods and receivables is liquidity unavailable to repay maturing debt; a firm that has just expanded its entire non-cash current asset base while a large share of its debt comes due within the year has converted repayment capacity into claims on customers and unsold product.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The archive's only fully aligned signal used inventory growth alone, but inventory is just one channel of working-capital lock-up — receivables are the other, and the two are substitutes across business models, so ranking their combined expansion should measure the underlying mechanism with less noise and less industry dependence. Both legs remain high-coverage annual items, so this should improve on the parent's 0.105 coverage while testing the same economics more completely.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Inventory Overhang State At The Maturity Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: What matters for a firm facing near-term maturities is not how fast inventory grew last year but whether the stock of goods is unusually large relative to the revenue it must generate; a firm sitting at the top of its own five-year inventory-to-sales range has an overhang that will only clear through discounting.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: This isolates a specific design choice on the archive's best joint signal — a persistent state versus a one-year flow — which matters because the flow version may work only through the accrual and asset-growth components it shares with published effects, whereas the state version is scaled by revenue and cannot be. If the state version retains the alpha and the slope, the mechanism is genuinely about stock overhang meeting rollover risk rather than about growth accounting.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Liquidity Lock-Up Against Composite Fragility
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(invt, 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(ceq, lt)))))
HYPOTHESIS: Rollover risk and a thin equity cushion are distinct fragilities that compound: a firm with debt maturing soon can survive if owners have capital at risk behind it, and a thinly capitalized firm can survive if nothing is due, but the firm exposed to both cannot absorb an inventory write-down.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The two conditioners that produced the archive's strongest alphas — the short-maturity share and the equity cushion — have never been combined, and because one measures the timing of claims while the other measures the capital behind them they should be complementary rather than redundant. Ranking their sum keeps the conditioner bounded and well-populated, preserving the aligned slope-and-alpha property of the inventory-growth investment leg.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Long And Lengthening Maturity With Sustained Investment
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent)), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), DELTA(RATIO(dlc, lt), 1)))))
HYPOTHESIS: Creditors reveal what they believe: a firm that is investing while its debt is both long-dated and getting longer has been granted funding on patient terms, and that endorsement is the resilience the market underprices; a firm investing while its maturity profile shortens is being financed only at the front end.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: Terming Out Debt While Still Investing was the first positive-sign signal in this archive to deliver a real alpha (+2.9%, t=+2.70), and its weakness is that a one-year change in maturity mix is noisy and can reflect a single refinancing; requiring the *level* to be long as well as the change to be lengthening identifies firms with durably patient capital. This is a substantive strengthening of the conditioner rather than a re-scaling of the investment leg.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Capacity Growth With Falling Labor Productivity
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(sale, emp), 1))))
HYPOTHESIS: Revenue per employee is the cleanest read on whether a firm's existing operations are working; adding plant while output per worker is deteriorating means the firm is scaling a process that is already losing efficiency, and the new capacity will dilute returns further.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Every distress leg in this archive is financial — leverage, maturity, liquidity, earnings, equity cushion — whereas operating efficiency measured on the labor base is an economic fragility that precedes the financial symptoms and is untested here. It also gives the generation one genuinely different axis, so a null result would tell us the interaction requires a balance-sheet constraint rather than merely deteriorating operations.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Asset-Liability Liquidity Mismatch
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(ppent, intan), at)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: Solvency under rollover pressure depends on how quickly assets can be turned into cash: a firm whose balance sheet is dominated by plant and intangibles — assets that take quarters to sell and sell at a discount when sold under duress — cannot meet a maturity wall from its own resources, regardless of how large its asset base looks.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The intangible-intensity version of this idea produced a -4.9% alpha with t=-4.07, but intangibles alone conflate pledgeability with liquidity and carry a known standalone effect; broadening the illiquid-asset measure to include fixed plant tests the liquidity-mismatch interpretation directly, since plant is pledgeable yet still slow to convert. A confirming result identifies asset-side illiquidity, not intangible intensity, as the operative characteristic.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---CRITIQUE Working Capital Lock-Up At The Maturity Wall---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: The two "distinct channels" are not distinct — (act − che) already contains inventory, so the SUMRANK double-counts the parent's leg rather than adding receivables information, and the resulting non-cash current-asset growth measure is essentially the working-capital accrual anomaly interacted with a conditioner already tested in the archive's "Inventory Buildup Against A Maturity Wall".

---CRITIQUE Inventory Overhang State At The Maturity Wall---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: A well-motivated state-versus-flow discrimination test: scaling inventory by sales and ranking against the firm's own five-year history strips out the growth-accounting/accrual component that could be driving the parent signal, so either outcome is informative about the mechanism.

---CRITIQUE Liquidity Lock-Up Against Composite Fragility---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: Internally consistent and the two conditioners are economically distinct (timing of claims versus capital behind them), but stacking two already-successful conditioners via SUMRANK is a fairly mechanical next step whose main risk is that averaging dilutes the sharper dlc/lt leg rather than compounding it.

---CRITIQUE Long And Lengthening Maturity With Sustained Investment---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: Sign and expression are aligned and adding the maturity level to the change is a defensible robustness strengthening, but the level term is large and slow-moving relative to the one-year change, so the signal risks collapsing into "capex by firms with little short-term debt" — a low-financial-constraint/quality composite — rather than testing the creditor-endorsement mechanism that produced the parent's alpha.

---CRITIQUE Capacity Growth With Falling Labor Productivity---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: This introduces the first genuinely operating (as opposed to balance-sheet) fragility axis in the archive, the sign matches the expression's direction, and a null result would be diagnostically useful; the main caveat is that emp coverage is thin and both legs individually border on the asset-growth and labor-hiring anomalies.

---CRITIQUE Asset-Liability Liquidity Mismatch---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: The stated purpose is to separate pledgeability from liquidity, but pooling ppent and intan into a single ratio confounds them further — ppent will dominate the measure for most firms — so this is a leg-rescaling of "Unpledgeable Assets Against Near-Term Maturities" that cannot deliver the discrimination it claims; ppent/at alone against dlc/lt would be the clean test.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Receivables Lock-Up At The Maturity Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(GROWTH(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), 1)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: If the mechanism behind the archive's best joint signal is genuinely about liquidity being locked into unconvertible assets, it should operate through receivables as well as goods: a firm that has extended far more credit to customers while a large share of its own debt matures within the year has financed its buyers instead of its lenders.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: Subtracting inventory as well as cash removes the double-count the critic identified and leaves a receivables-and-other-current-asset channel that is genuinely disjoint from the parent signal's leg, making this a discrimination test rather than a re-pairing. If it works, the mechanism is general working-capital lock-up meeting rollover risk; if only the inventory version works, the effect is about unsold product specifically, and either answer directs the final generations.

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Operating Intangibles Against Near-Term Maturities
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(intan, COALESCE(gdwl, 0)), at)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: Intangible assets excluding acquisition goodwill — capitalized software, patents, licences — are the assets a lender will not take as security and a buyer will not pay for in a hurry; a firm whose balance sheet is built on them and whose debt matures within the year has no collateral to post when the refinancing conversation begins.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: Pooling plant with intangibles would have confounded pledgeability further, so instead this strips goodwill out of the intangible measure, which directly tests the critic's concern that the -4.9% alpha of the parent signal may be inherited from acquisition legacy rather than from collateral quality. Treating an unreported goodwill balance as zero is the correct accounting convention here, and the residual non-goodwill intangible intensity is the cleanest available proxy for unpledgeable operating assets.
